final_proof:
Let C(I) denote the set of all continuous functions f:I→ℝ, and define the two operations by (f+g)(x)=f(x)+g(x) and (α·f)(x)=αf(x) for x∈I and α∈ℝ. We first verify that these operations are internal in the required sense. If f,g∈C(I), x₀∈I, and ε>0, continuity of f and g at x₀ gives positive numbers δ_f and δ_g such that, for y∈I, |y−x₀|<δ_f implies |f(y)−f(x₀)|<ε/2 and |y−x₀|<δ_g implies |g(y)−g(x₀)|<ε/2. Hence, with δ=min{δ_f,δ_g}, we have |(f+g)(y)−(f+g)(x₀)|≤|f(y)−f(x₀)|+|g(y)−g(x₀)|<ε whenever y∈I and |y−x₀|<δ. Thus f+g∈C(I). If α∈ℝ and f∈C(I), then α·f is continuous: this is immediate when α=0, while for α≠0 continuity of f with tolerance ε/|α| gives |αf(y)−αf(x₀)|<ε. Therefore scalar multiplication also maps ℝ×C(I) into C(I).

Define 0_I:I→ℝ by 0_I(x)=0. This constant function is continuous, so C(I) is nonempty. For every f∈C(I), the function −f=(−1)·f is continuous by the scalar-closure result above. Pointwise, (f+0_I)(x)=f(x)+0=f(x) and (f+(−f))(x)=f(x)−f(x)=0=0_I(x). Hence 0_I is an additive identity and −f is an additive inverse of f.

It remains to check the remaining vector-space identities. Let f,g,h∈C(I), let α,β∈ℝ, and let x∈I. The field identities in ℝ give
((f+g)+h)(x)=(f(x)+g(x))+h(x)=f(x)+(g(x)+h(x))=(f+(g+h))(x),
(f+g)(x)=f(x)+g(x)=g(x)+f(x)=(g+f)(x),
(α·(f+g))(x)=α(f(x)+g(x))=αf(x)+αg(x)=((α·f)+(α·g))(x),
((α+β)·f)(x)=(α+β)f(x)=αf(x)+βf(x)=((α·f)+(β·f))(x),
((αβ)·f)(x)=(αβ)f(x)=α(βf(x))=(α·(β·f))(x),
and (1·f)(x)=1f(x)=f(x). Because the two functions in each displayed identity agree at every x∈I, they are equal. Thus pointwise addition is associative and commutative, the two distributive laws hold, scalar multiplication is compatible with multiplication in ℝ, and 1 acts as the scalar identity. Together with closure, the zero function, and additive inverses proved above, these are all the vector-space axioms. Consequently (C(I),+,·) is a vector space over ℝ.
